title: Pandas and Dataset Preparation: Read, Filter, Join, Group, Transform
description: Prepare structured datasets safely and understand how pandas operations change row counts, columns, and dtypes.
learningObjectives: Inspect a DataFrame's shape, columns, dtypes, and representative rows before transforming it.
Use filtering, column selection, merge, groupby, and transformations with predictable outputs.
Detect join multiplication and validate expected relationship cardinality.
Explain why dataset transformations should preserve lineage and be reproducible.

mentalModel.text: A DataFrame is a labelled table. Every operation can change rows, columns, order, or types, so good dataset preparation checks what changed instead of assuming the table still represents the same records.

blocks.title: Read and inspect a CSV
blocks.source:
from io import StringIO
import pandas as pd

csv_text = """ticket_id,status,priority
T-101,open,high
T-102,closed,low
T-103,open,medium
"""
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv_text))
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.head(3).to_string(index=False))

blocks.text: This is a self-contained example: `StringIO` makes the sample text behave like a CSV file. Expected output begins with `(3, 3)`, then shows the inferred dtype for each column, followed by T-101, T-102, and T-103. The exact dtype labels can vary by pandas version and dtype configuration; the row/column shape and IDs are deterministic. Trace: `read_csv` parses the header into column names, infers types, and loads three rows; `shape`, `dtypes`, and `head` inspect it without changing it.

`shape` reports `(rows, columns)`, `dtypes` exposes inferred column types, and `head()` shows representative records. Also inspect key uniqueness, null counts, and ranges before assuming a column is numeric or an ID is unique.

blocks.title: Select and filter with an explicit condition

blocks.text: Using the `df` built in the preceding example, the result contains exactly two rows: `T-101 high` and `T-103 medium`. `.eq('open')` creates a Boolean condition, `.loc` keeps only matching rows, and the column list selects `ticket_id` and `priority`. The output depends on the input data; this preceding sample makes it reproducible.
The first condition selects open rows; the second argument chooses two columns. `.loc` makes the row and column selection explicit and avoids carrying unrelated fields through every later step.

blocks.title: Join tickets to one row per customer
blocks.source:
import pandas as pd

tickets = pd.DataFrame({
    "ticket_id": ["T-101", "T-102", "T-103"],
    "customer_id": ["C1", "C2", "C1"],
})
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": ["C1", "C2"],
    "plan": ["pro", "starter"],
})

result = tickets.merge(
    customers,
    on="customer_id",
    how="left",
    validate="many_to_one",
)
print(len(tickets), len(result))
print(result.to_string(index=False))

blocks.text: Expected first line: `3 3`. The output has three tickets, each joined to exactly one customer: T-101→C1/pro, T-102→C2/starter, and T-103→C1/pro. `many_to_one` validates that the customer side has at most one row per customer ID. If a duplicate `C1` row is added to `customers`, pandas raises a `MergeError` rather than silently multiplying ticket rows.

If each ticket should map to at most one customer row, `validate='many_to_one'` checks that the right side is unique by the join key. If it is not, pandas raises an error instead of silently multiplying ticket rows.

blocks.problem: There are 1,000 tickets and the customer table contains two rows for customer 42.
reasoning: A ticket for customer 42 matches both customer rows in an ordinary merge.
Those tickets can appear twice in the output, so aggregate counts or class frequencies may become inflated.
Check duplicate keys and the intended relationship; use merge validation where possible, then compare row counts and unmatched keys.
blocks.outcome: Do not accept a merge just because it ran. State whether the relationship is one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-one and validate that assumption.

blocks.title: Aggregate to customer level
blocks.source:
import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame({
    "event_id": ["e1", "e2", "e3"],
    "customer_id": ["C1", "C1", "C2"],
    "amount": [10, 15, 7],
})
summary = (
    events.groupby("customer_id", as_index=False)
          .agg(event_count=("event_id", "count"),
               spend_total=("amount", "sum"))
)
print(summary.to_string(index=False))

blocks.text: Expected output is two rows: customer C1 has `event_count=2` and `spend_total=25`; C2 has `event_count=1` and `spend_total=7`. The input has three event rows, but `agg` returns one row per customer group. The amounts are summed within each group.
`groupby(...).agg(...)` returns one row per customer group. That is appropriate for customer-level summaries, but it no longer has one row per event.

blocks.title: Add a group statistic while preserving event rows
blocks.source:
import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame({
    "event_id": ["e1", "e2", "e3"],
    "customer_id": ["C1", "C1", "C2"],
    "amount": [10, 15, 7],
})
events = events.copy()
events["customer_total"] = events.groupby("customer_id")["amount"].transform("sum")
print(events.to_string(index=False))

blocks.text: Expected output preserves all three events and adds `customer_total`: e1/C1/10/25, e2/C1/15/25, and e3/C2/7/7. `transform('sum')` computes a sum per customer and aligns it back to each original row; it does not reduce the table's grain.
`transform` returns a value aligned to the original rows, so every event receives its customer's total. This is different from `agg`, which reduces the table to one row per group.

A data pipeline should make it possible to explain where rows disappeared or multiplied. Capture input row counts, filter counts, duplicate-key counts, merge coverage, null counts, and final output shape. A transformation that produces a plausible-looking result can still be wrong.

blocks.title: Questions to ask after each step
rows: Filtering, exploding, joins, and grouping can change cardinality.
Numbers read as text can break sorting and calculations.
Duplicate keys can multiply rows or make updates ambiguous.
Joins and coercion can introduce new nulls.
Reproducible inputs and explicit transformations help debugging.

blocks.title: Do not patch data quality silently
blocks.content: Avoid silently coercing invalid values to zero or dropping all rows with any null. Record the rule and counts, preserve important IDs, and verify the result before sending it to a model.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.text: Pandas is convenient for medium-sized in-memory analysis, but memory use can grow through copies and wide joins. For data larger than memory, consider chunked processing or a database/stream engine instead of forcing the entire dataset into one DataFrame.

revisionSheet.text: Inspect `shape`, `dtypes`, null counts, key uniqueness, and `head()` before transforming.
Use `merge(validate=...)` to catch unexpected join cardinality.
`agg` usually reduces rows; `transform` aligns results back to input rows.
Compare row counts, duplicate keys, unmatched keys, and null counts after consequential steps.

questions.prompt: A merge unexpectedly doubles the number of event rows. What is a likely cause?

options.text: The right-side join key contains multiple matching rows
Pandas always duplicates all rows in a left join
The CSV encoding is necessarily wrong

questions.explanation: A many-to-many or unexpected one-to-many relationship can multiply matched rows.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of `merge(..., validate='many_to_one')` when joining events to customers?

options.text: It checks that the right-side join key is unique as expected
It sorts the events by time automatically
It fills missing customers with zeros

questions.explanation: Merge validation checks the expected key relationship and surfaces duplicates rather than silently allowing multiplication.

questions.prompt: Which operation is designed to calculate a group-level sum and keep one output row per customer?
questions.explanation: Aggregation reduces each group to a summary row.

questions.prompt: You need each event row to include the total amount for its customer without reducing the event-level row count. Which concept is suitable?
questions.explanation: Transform produces results aligned to the original rows.

questions.prompt: A successful pandas merge proves that the join keys and relationship were correct.
questions.explanation: The merge can succeed with wrong cardinality or unmatched keys; validate assumptions and inspect the output.

questions.prompt: Checking row counts and key uniqueness after a merge can reveal problems that are invisible in a few preview rows.
questions.explanation: Summary checks are necessary because small samples may not expose duplicate-key multiplication or systematic unmatched records.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A training dataset suddenly reports twice as many positive examples after joining events to customer metadata.
strongAnswerPoints: Check uniqueness of customer IDs in the metadata table.
Use merge validation and count rows before/after; inspect keys with multiple matches.
Fix duplicate source keys or define an intentional aggregation/deduplication rule.
pitfalls: Assuming the model data improved because there are more rows
Dropping duplicates without deciding which customer record is authoritative
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would suspect join multiplication first. I would verify customer-key uniqueness and the intended relationship, then validate the merge and recount class labels.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A pipeline groups event data by customer and downstream code can no longer find `event_id` for individual events.
strongAnswerPoints: Explain that groupby/agg reduced to one row per group.
Use transform if the statistic must be attached to each event, or keep separate event and summary tables.
Document the row grain expected by each downstream stage.
pitfalls: Trying to recreate original detail from an aggregated table without a join
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: The aggregate changed the grain from event-level to customer-level. I'd preserve the event table and either use transform or join a customer summary back to the event rows.
